title: Kup Rahira, February 1762
hook: in the great holocaust, the Khalsa formed a moving ring round its families, and very many died

segments.voice: Yesterday, women carried off after Panipat were freed and walked back to their own families. Your line was brought home safe. Did you stay with someone until they were steady? Today, families of their own, and a hard day. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

For years the Khalsa had stayed alive by being fast. A band of horsemen could strike and be gone before an army turned around. Speed was their shelter. Now look at the column crossing the fields near two villages called Kup and Rahira. It isn't fast at all. It's carts and cattle and grandparents and children, moving at the pace of the slowest walker. And riding alongside it are fighters who have lived by speed, going slow on purpose. Then an army appears. Today: Kup Rahira.
screen: `SPEED WAS THEIR SHELTER.` → `A COLUMN AT A WALKING PACE.` → `THE FAST RIDE SLOW.`

segments.voice: Sikhs call a moving camp of families like this a vahir. Children, elders, the cooking pots, everything. The great holocaust has been told before: the surprise, the ring, the terrible losses. Today, look at one choice inside that day. When Abdali's army caught the vahir, the fighters had a way out. Horsemen can scatter. They'd done it for years. Split up, ride hard, regroup later. Some of them might have got away. Tradition says they didn't. They formed a ring around the families, fought on the outside, and kept the whole column moving forward together, at the pace of its slowest people. Riders would turn and charge to push the attackers back, then return to the ring. Again and again, all day. That's what a shield is. Not the strongest thing on the battlefield, but the thing that stays between the danger and the ones who can't run. And the cost was enormous. Very many died that day, fighters and families both. This lesson gives no figure. It remembers the people. Why stay? Sikh teaching holds that the Khalsa is there to protect the defenseless, and these weren't strangers. They were mothers, fathers, children. The Ardas, said at the close of gurdwara gatherings, remembers those who gave their lives rather than give up their faith. Sikhs hold the dead of Kup Rahira among the ones it carries. It's not a story with a clever twist. It's a story about staying. The fast rode slow, and they shielded the families.
screen: `A VAHIR: A MOVING CAMP OF FAMILIES.` · `THE FIGHTERS COULD HAVE SCATTERED.` · `A RING THAT KEPT WALKING.` · `REMEMBERED IN THE ARDAS.` · then, large: `THEY SHIELDED THE FAMILIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a minute of silence, and then the rest of the bell. Sit still. Let your hands rest. For the first minute, don't think about anything in particular. Just keep a silence for the people of that day, fighters and families, whose names you may never learn. When the minute has passed, let one person come to mind: someone you would step in front of if harm came. Just hold them there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, softly, at the end. The bell holds the time.
Kup Rahira. The place, named for two villages, where the Khalsa formed a moving ring around its families against Abdali's army, and very many died. Today's word.
Your line: they shielded the families. Today, slow down for the slowest person with you, and stay between them and whatever's coming. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Vadda Ghallughara, the great holocaust fought near Kup and Rahira, in the Ardas and at commemorations, honoring those who died shielding the families.

fork.setup: you're a Sikh horseman. an army has caught your people's slow column of families in the open. your horse is fast. what do you do?
options: scatter and ride hard, as you've always done.
form a ring around the families and keep them moving.
fork.reveal: tradition says the fighters formed a moving ring and kept the families walking all day, at a terrible cost.

original.note: Gurmukhi: vahir, a moving camp or caravan of people with their families and belongings.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kup Rahira was a battle.
what it means: it was a moving ring of fighters shielding a column of families, at a walking pace, all day.
what a scholar hears: horsemen who had survived by speed chose to stay with the slow vahir, and the Ardas carries the memory of those who died.
